methods.label: Apply each speaker's truth rule
methods.explanation:
Chris and LeRoy cannot both be toads, because each would falsely call the other a frog. They cannot both be frogs, because each would truthfully call the other a frog. Thus exactly one of Chris and LeRoy is a toad.

Now consider Brian's two possible species. If Brian is a toad, his claim that he and Mike are different species is true, so Mike is a frog. If Brian is a frog, his claim is false, so Mike is the same species as Brian and is again a frog. These cases exhaust Brian's possibilities, so Mike must be a frog.

Mike's statement is therefore false: fewer than two of the four amphibians are toads. Chris and LeRoy already include one toad, so Brian must be a frog as well.

These conclusions are consistent: Brian and Mike both make false statements, while either choice of the toad among Chris and LeRoy makes both of their statements obey their species' rules. In either assignment there is one toad and \(\boxed{3}\) frogs, choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
